<strong>À l’occasion de la Semaine de se: On the occasion of Muslim Awareness Week and the National Day of Remembrance of the Quebec City Mosque Attack and of Action against Islamophobia, Amira Elghawaby sat down with La Converse. Canada’s Special Representative on Combatting Islamophobia explains her role, responds to criticism and opens up about her own experiences as a woman who wears the hijab and holds a public role in Canada. Interview.
C’est dans ses bureaux, nichés au cinqui: Amira Elghawaby welcomed our journalist and the students of École Converse for an in-depth interview in her offices, tucked away on the fifth floor of a federal government administration building in Ottawa. While the agent at the front desk doesn’t seem to know her name, Canada’s Special Representative on Combatting Islamophobia regularly makes headlines, particularly in Quebec. That doesn’t stop this former journalist, supported by a team of 10 people dedicated to fighting Islamophobia, from continuing to play along with the interview game.
<strong>Pourquoi avoir accepté la foncti: Why did you accept the role of Canada’s Special Representative on Combatting Islamophobia?
J’ai grandi ici, à Ottawa, et j’ai eu un: I grew up here in Ottawa, and I had a very privileged youth. Even as the daughter of Egyptian immigrants, I was always encouraged at school to share my different identities. As the daughter of Egyptian parents, my faith and these identities were always seen in a very positive way. I always hoped that growing up in Canada meant being in a place where I could be fully authentic.
« Mes enfants me posaient des questions: “My children used to ask me questions like, ‘Why do people hate us?’ No parent should ever have to answer that question…” – Amira Elghawaby
C’est à l’université que j’ai décidé de: It was at university that I decided to start wearing the hijab, and it was my father who said to me, “Be careful, you could be a victim of discrimination!” I remember thinking, “No, we’re in Canada. If I can’t be authentic about who I am and my identity here, then where in the world could I be?”
À l’époque, je n’avais jamais entendu le: At the time, I had never heard the word “Islamophobia”! I had many, many positive experiences at school, where principals and teachers encouraged me to share who I was. Everything changed after September 11. It made me aware of the different forms of discrimination people can face here in Canada.
Lorsqu’on m’a offert ce poste, cela m’a: When I was offered this position, it really spoke to me, because it makes it possible to confront a serious phenomenon: Islamophobia. My children used to ask me questions like “Why do people hate us?” No parent should ever have to answer that question…
<strong>En quoi consiste votre fonction: What does your role as Special Representative involve?
Mon rôle consiste à garantir un canal de: My role is to ensure a direct channel of communication between Canadian Muslims and federal ministers, including the prime minister. I provide advice on how policies affect people’s everyday lives, and I help federal departments tackle systemic forms of Islamophobia.
Un autre aspect clé de mon rôle est la s: Another key part of my role is awareness-raising, through interviews like this one, discussions on media platforms and federal anti-racism initiatives. I also work to provide resources, including a guide on Islamophobia – which will be published soon – and materials meant to help communities fight hate crimes.
<strong>Au début de votre mandat, des ap: At the start of your mandate, there were calls for your resignation, particularly in Quebec. How did you handle that?
Lorsque ma nomination a été annoncée, le: When my appointment was announced, Canadian Muslims from coast to coast expressed incredible hope. Of course, we expected there would be criticism and discussion about things I had written in the past. What I did – and what anyone in this position should do – was listen. I listened to the concerns that were raised and acknowledged the impact words can have. It was important to have a dialogue, to clear up misunderstandings and to move forward with the important work ahead of us.
Je pense que chaque province a une histo: I think every province has its own history and realities, and I acknowledge some people’s concerns. However, the vast majority of Canadians – whether they live in Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba or the Atlantic provinces – value inclusion and fairness. Those are the values we need to focus on. So I rolled up my sleeves and got to work.
<strong>En cette septième Semaine de la: For this seventh Muslim Awareness Week, what is your message?
Parfois, nous voyons des récits négatifs: Sometimes we see negative stories about our communities in the media, on social media, in newspapers or on television and radio. And we wonder, “Who are they talking about?” Because it’s not us… We are Canadians like everyone else. We wake up in the morning, we get our kids ready for school – if we have any – or we get ready for work or school, and we head out determined to do our best, not only for ourselves and our families, but also for society as a whole.
As I see it, there are two paths before us. One is the path of polarization and division, where we distrust one another and create laws that limit rights and freedoms. The other is the path of inclusion, where we respect one another.
<strong>Comment a évolué la lutte contre: How has the fight against Islamophobia in Canada evolved in recent years?
Nous aimerions qu’elle soit éliminée, ma: We would like it to be eliminated, but the reality is that hatred, division and racism still exist. If we look at the past few years, we remember January 29, 2017: the night six Canadian Muslims were murdered in cold blood, simply for attending prayer at their mosque. Where are we today?
Malheureusement, les espaces en ligne so: Unfortunately, online spaces have become a major factor in the spread of hate. Over the past year and a half, at times we have seen increases of more than 400% in anti-Muslim narratives online. These attacks are not only about Islamophobia, but also about rejecting conversations on equity, diversity and inclusion, and trying to stifle those discussions.
<strong>Vous êtes une femme, une musulma: You are a woman, a Muslim, a hijabi and a public figure. What is your personal experience of Islamophobia?
Mon expérience est que j’ai été confront: My experience is that over the years, and as recently as last weekend, I have faced harassment and Islamophobic speech – and I have been told things that were truly, truly offensive. Things I won’t repeat here, because I don’t want to relive them and I don’t want to harm those who are listening to me either. If we dwell too much on what those who want to spread hate say, we risk losing hope in the way we function and take part in the life of society.
Il y a quelques années, un camion m’a pr: A few years ago, a truck almost deliberately hit me, just after I’d had my first child, while I was walking in my neighbourhood here in Ottawa. I never reported it to the police, as is the case for many victims of hate crimes. I was simply scared and ran home.
J’ai vécu ces expériences, mais en même: I have lived through these experiences, but at the same time, it is very important for me to say that for every negative experience I’ve had while wearing the hijab, I have also had many very positive ones. Very recently, when I was harassed, several people who witnessed it came up to me and said, “That’s not right, we’re with you. What do you need? We want to help you.” Yes, I have faced Islamophobia on a personal level, but I have also benefited from the support of a great ally.
<strong>L’attentat de la mosquée de Québ: The Quebec City mosque attack was a tragic moment in Canadian history. Why is it important to keep commemorating it?
J’ai rencontré les familles des victimes: I met with the families of the victims of the massacre last weekend, and I can tell you what the widows told me. They told me it’s important that this work continues, and that it means a lot to them and to their children that there is this national recognition of what happened. These national days exist so that we remember and so that we learn from history. What did we learn on January 29?
Nous avons appris que les discours négat: We learned that negative speech and hate on the internet cause divisions in our societies. We learned that what our elected leaders say matters. The perpetrator of the January 29 attack consumed a lot of hate against minorities on various platforms. He acted after the prime minister of Canada posted a tweet in response to President Donald Trump’s Muslim Ban. In that tweet, the prime minister had mentioned that here, “Canada is a place where everyone is welcome.”
C’est ce qui a fait basculer le meurtrie: That is what tipped the murderer, the terrorist, over the edge; it is what drove him to commit this horrific crime. Everything was built on the argument that Muslims are a danger; he wanted to “protect his family” from everything he had wrongly heard about Muslims. He was unable to tell truth from lies.
<strong>Quelle a été l’influence de cet: What influence has this event had on public policy and on discussions about Islamophobia in Canadian society?
Je travaille sur l’islamophobie depuis a: I have been working on Islamophobia since at least 2012 in a variety of spaces. I can tell you that we have been able to make progress and that we have been using the term “Islamophobia” for a little while now. There has been a lot of pushback over the use of the term “Islamophobia,” but we insisted that we are experiencing this hatred, this discrimination. It is Islamophobia. People have an irrational fear of Muslims. They share all this false information. Some in the public space say, “Are you saying we can’t criticize Islam? That will harm our freedom of expression.” I answer them, “No, of course, criticize Islam, criticize whatever you want, but don’t defame Canadian Muslims, Quebec Muslims or any Muslim.”
Cela a pris le meurtre de 11 Canadiens m: It took the murder of 11 Canadian Muslims for people to understand that. It shouldn’t have taken this long. We should have had more help and more support before this happened. It took the loss of a family in London, of Muslims in Quebec City and of the man who was stabbed outside the mosque in 2020. It took all these tragic losses for people to wake up and realize this is truly serious.
<strong>Depuis le 7 octobre 2023, quelle: Since October 7, 2023, what impact has the war between Israel and Palestine had on Muslim communities in Canada?
Au cours de l’année et demie écoulée, de: Over the past year and a half, since October 7, we have seen a significant rise in anti-Palestinian racism, Islamophobia, anti-Arab racism, as well as antisemitism – and we condemn all of it. None of it is acceptable. And I think our communities have been tested in different ways. One of the very first statements I made for my office was to say that Canadian Muslims were not going to allow a return to the period right after September 11, when we had to apologize and explain things that had nothing to do with us.
J’ai entendu parler de certains cas, not: I have heard about certain cases, including that of a public servant from Gaza who went through very difficult times just thinking about and going back over what she had endured after seeing what was happening to her loved ones. And right here in Ottawa, she is facing repercussions at work simply because she spoke about the emotional toll she was feeling. That is not acceptable!
<strong>Pourquoi est-il important, selon: Why do you think it is important for Canada to recognize anti-Palestinian racism?
Je sais que les Canado-Palestiniens qui: I know that Palestinian Canadians who are Muslim, but also Christian, are going to be victims of anti-Palestinian racism that is linked to, and can be connected to, Islamophobia, but is also distinct. It has been very important for my office to make sure we help inform Canadians about this distinct form of discrimination.
J’ai un grand d’espoir après avoir enten: I have great hope after hearing the prime minister’s commitment, from his own mouth, to define anti-Palestinian racism at the federal level. That is very important, because for a year and a half, efforts have been made to silence those who speak about anti-Palestinian racism.
Dans une école d’Ottawa, par exemple, un: At an Ottawa school, for example, an elementary school student logged on to the internet, put a small photo of the Palestinian flag on their profile, and the school principal reprimanded this child online, saying they were creating a climate of insecurity for the other students. The student then replied, “I’m the one who doesn’t feel safe.” The principal ended up apologizing, because Palestinian identity is their identity, they are Palestinian Canadians, and they have the right to have that identity.
<strong>Dans le contexte actuel de polar: In the current context of polarization and incomprehension, are you working with Jewish communities to establish a dialogue?
Je sais que la période a été très, très: I know that this period has been very, very difficult for Muslims, Arabs and Palestinian Canadians, as well as for Canadian Jewish communities. I have very dear friends in the Canadian Jewish community. We cried with one of them because the discourse about relations between Jews and Muslims has been so negative and so conflictual, when religions teach love, compassion and respect.
Nous espérons que le cessez-le-feu tiend: We hope the ceasefire will hold and that peace will slowly return, but there is no peace without justice. This is an important element of this discourse. It’s not just about ending the war, but also about making sure that the lives of international humanitarian workers are respected and protected. How can we establish interfaith dialogues with communities if we can’t first establish respect for human rights among ourselves?
<strong>Récemment, nous avons appris que: We recently learned that the Supreme Court will hear the challenge to the Quebec government’s Bill 21. What do you think of that decision?
Ce que j’ai entendu haut et fort lors de: What I have heard loud and clear during my visits to Quebec is that Bill 21 has had a very negative effect on Muslim women’s sense of belonging, on their sense of safety in the province. That is what comes out of various surveys and studies. We also saw a lower court judge in Quebec say that the law had a disproportionate effect on Muslim women in Quebec, an effect he even described as cruel.
Ce que j’ai entendu, depuis l’annonce de: What I have heard since the announcement of the Supreme Court of Canada’s decision to hear the case – in which the federal government will also intervene – is that there is hope. There is hope that our rights and freedoms as Canadians will not be undermined, devalued. I think that is very important for Canadians. Everyone must be able to enjoy the same rights and freedoms.
Lorsque je me lève le matin, je devrais: When I get up in the morning, I should be able to wear what I want and take full part in the life of society. I shouldn’t have to tell a little girl or a little boy who wants to become a teacher or a police officer that this profession might be closed to them because of how they decide to practise their faith when they’re an adult. That is not the kind of Canada we want, and it is not what we are aiming for with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
<strong>Nous observons actuellement, au: We are currently seeing a rise in conservatism in Canada, but also in the rest of the world. Are you afraid this will make Islamophobia worse?
Avec une polarisation de plus en plus fo: With ever-stronger polarization in the world, where there are more and more spaces in which division is truly part of the discourse, we know that algorithms sometimes amplify messages and content that make people angry. It’s very worrying. Last summer, the federal government published a report stating that the main threat to Canadians is the inability to tell what is true from what is not. All of these trends are therefore very concerning for anyone who cares about social cohesion, bringing people together and truth. Like everyone who is watching these trends, I am deeply worried.
<strong>À propos du Canada, ne craignez-: Speaking of Canada, aren’t you afraid that a new government could jeopardize the very existence of your office to combat Islamophobia?
Mon rôle est celui d’un conseiller indép: My role is that of an independent, non-partisan adviser to the federal government. My job is to provide advice, and I will continue to do so, since my mandate is four years. Whatever happens at the government level, we take things day by day. But as long as my mandate remains in effect, I will do my best for Canadians to advance a society in which Islamophobia and all forms of hate and racism are fought.
<strong>En 2021, le Sommet national sur: In 2021, the National Summit on Islamophobia made 61 recommendations. Have they been implemented?
Un an après le sommet, le Conseil nation: One year after the summit, the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM) published a report assessing the implementation of those recommendations. It found that at least 30% of them had been implemented or were being carried out, and efforts are currently under way to increase that figure. In the meantime, other reports have been devoted to Islamophobia, including a Senate report and a Justice Committee report that examined its link to anti-Palestinian and anti-Arab racism, forms of discrimination that have increased considerably over the past year.
